verdict.root_cause: The frontend is not at fault: every error it logs is an outbound gRPC connection failure to a single peer, 172.18.0.19:9555, the ad service's port, escalating from ECONNREFUSED to EHOSTUNREACH [tr_7aa78830adfe]. The ad service's change log shows an automated policy repeatedly clamping its memory limit to 144m and restoring it, with the latest clamp five minutes before onset and never restored [tr_e28af516e347]. That is the signature of a callee being killed for exceeding its memory cap: the endpoint stops accepting, the caller sees refused connections, and the ad hop emits no spans at all across 174 sampled spans [tr_04ece1c3b26b]. Only ad-bearing paths fail, which is why the frontend error ratio rises ~1.67x and peaks at 0.093 without locking high [tr_45251a674f30]. The limit edit is how it started; running out of memory is what is happening.
verdict.reasoning: The frontend log names exactly one dependency, by IP and port, in every error line, which excludes an internal frontend bug and a multi-dependency failure [tr_7aa78830adfe]. The only change on that service in the entire retention window is a cycling 144m memory cap, last applied five minutes before onset with no restoration — no deploy, no flag, no scale-down [tr_e28af516e347]. Refused connections rather than error responses point to a process that is dead or restarting, not slow. The trace specialist read ad's absence from all traces as exoneration; I read it as corroboration, since an OOM-killed callee emits no spans [tr_04ece1c3b26b]. The partial error elevation fits one missing fan-out leg [tr_45251a674f30]. The two dispatches finding ad healthy queried 03:50-09:50 [tr_48b01b06585b, tr_9071767761cf] — a window ending an hour before the incident begins — so they are baseline, not refutation. Reverting the limit is the fix; a restart alone would be re-killed by the same cap.
open_questions: No ad logs or metrics were gathered inside the actual incident window (10:20-10:52); OOM-kill or restart events there would confirm the mechanism directly, and without them the link from the 144m cap to the refused connections is inferred.
The mapping of 172.18.0.19:9555 to the ad service rests on port convention, not a verified service-to-IP lookup; if that port belongs to another workload, blame moves with it.
The shift from ECONNREFUSED to EHOSTUNREACH is unexplained by a simple kill loop — refused implies a host with nothing listening, unreachable implies the host or route is gone.

alternatives.root_cause: The ad service's container lost its network attachment or was descheduled, leaving it running but unreachable from the frontend.
alternatives.why_not: A partition does not explain the memory-cap change landing five minutes before onset, and the early ECONNREFUSED indicates a reachable host with no listener rather than a severed route.

alternatives.root_cause: product-catalog latency is the real driver of frontend degradation, flagged as the degrading hop in four traces.
alternatives.why_not: Single-digit-millisecond self-times cannot produce gRPC UNAVAILABLE errors, and the frontend's log names no address but the one on port 9555.

proposal.expected_effect: Restoring the ad service's previous resource configuration (memory limit = None, the recorded prior state before the 10:45:30 clamp to 144m) and recreating the container should put a listener back on port 9555. Observable as: (1) frontend logs stop emitting new `14 UNAVAILABLE ... connect ECONNREFUSED/EHOSTUNREACH 172.18.0.19:9555` lines within a few minutes of the recreate — the embedded last-error timestamp stops advancing; (2) ad spans reappear under frontend in Tempo traces on ad-bearing paths (currently zero ad spans in 174 sampled spans); (3) the frontend error ratio returns toward its 0.025 baseline mean with peaks well under the observed 0.093.
proposal.if_wrong: Falsified if, 10 minutes after the recreate, frontend still logs fresh connection failures to 172.18.0.19:9555 with an advancing last-error timestamp, or if ad spans are still absent from frontend traces. In particular, persistence of EHOSTUNREACH (rather than ECONNREFUSED) after the revert would indicate the host/route is gone — a network detach, not a memory cap — which this action cannot fix and which the permitted action set does not cover (reconnect_service is unavailable). Also falsified if ad logs/metrics inside 10:20–10:52 show no OOM-kill or restart activity at all, which would break the inferred link from the 144m cap to the refused connections; that evidence was never gathered. A third falsifier: the frontend error ratio stays at ~0.042 while ad spans return, meaning the errors came from a different workload that happens to own 172.18.0.19:9555 (the IP-to-service mapping rests on port convention, not a verified lookup).
proposal.risk: If the diagnosis is wrong, this is a container recreate of a healthy ad service for no benefit: in-flight ad requests are dropped and any in-process ad cache is lost, briefly worsening the very error ratio we are trying to lower. Removing the memory cap is not free — the automated policy applied 144m four times in one day, and if the ad service has a genuine memory leak, lifting the ceiling lets it grow unbounded and apply memory pressure to co-located containers on the same host rather than being contained by an OOM kill. The policy itself is not changed by this action, so platform-automation may re-clamp to 144m and reproduce the fault; this is a symptom revert, not a fix of the loop.
proposal.blast_radius: The ad service only, plus its inbound callers. frontend is the named caller of ad and will see connection resets for the seconds the container recreates — already failing on these paths, so the marginal harm is small. Through frontend, frontend-proxy and the load-generator's ad-bearing page loads see the same window. cart, checkout, product-catalog, product-reviews and recommendation are untouched; no dependency address is being changed, so no traffic moves to other services.

triage_judgement.reasoning: Critical alerts on frontend and its proxy simultaneously, with no open incident to attribute them to, affect user-facing traffic and cannot be dismissed. The simultaneous seed pair suggests a shared downstream dependency, but nothing in the alerts identifies a class yet.
